title: No-thought
hookLine: Huineng: no-thought is not blankness but not being stuck to thoughts

cards: A big station has a departures board. Every few minutes it clicks over: a new train, a new platform, a new city. Nobody standing in the hall gets on every train.
Most people glance up, read a line, and keep walking. Some trains they board. Most they let go, and the board doesn't mind either way.

Now try that with a mind. Thoughts click over all day: lunch, that email, a worry about Thursday. Huineng had a word for meeting them the way a traveler meets a departures board, and it's probably not what it sounds like.

teach.b: In the Platform Sutra, Huineng sets out three teachings side by side: no-thought as the doctrine, no-form as the substance, and non-abiding as the root. Today is the first, but they lean on each other.
No-thought sounds like an empty head, a mind wiped blank. Huineng says plainly that this is a mistake.
Trying to think of nothing at all, cutting off every thought, is in his telling its own kind of trap, a mind tied up by an idea of what meditation should be. So what is it?
In paraphrase, he says no-thought means that in the midst of thoughts, you are not carried off by them.
Thought follows thought, and none of them is held on to. That's the non-abiding: the mind doesn't move in and live in any one of them. When thoughts don't stick, he says, there is no bondage.
So the worry about Thursday can arrive, can even be useful, and then go, the way a train leaves the board. And the senses stay open. Huineng doesn't ask anyone to close their eyes on the world.

teach.h: THE SENSES COME AND GO FREELY.
teach.b: He describes the senses going out and coming back freely, seeing and hearing everything, while the mind isn't stained by what it meets. No-thought, in his hands, isn't less life. It's full life, with nothing gripping.
The same thread the Xinxin Ming was pulling a few days ago, now tied to a teacher's seat: not stuck.

how: Zen and Chan teachers often explain Huineng's no-thought in talks on sitting, describing practice as letting thoughts arise and pass without being carried off, rather than forcing the mind blank.

o: meeting thoughts without being carried off
letting thoughts carry you wherever they go
a mind wiped completely blank of thinking

s: for Huineng, no-thought means stopping all thinking
he says it means not being carried off by thoughts, and warns against forcing the mind blank.
Huineng pairs no-thought with no-form and non-abiding
he sets the three side by side as doctrine, substance and root.
no-thought means closing off the senses
he describes the senses going out and coming back freely, with the mind unstained.

games.q: you're sitting, and a worry about Thursday's meeting shows up. by Huineng's teaching, what now?
o: shove it out and make the mind blank
let it arrive and go without boarding it
follow it all the way to the end to be done with it
games.why: Huineng calls forcing the mind blank a mistake. no-thought is meeting the thought without being carried off.

practice: Don't try to stop thinking; let thoughts come up like lines on a departures board, notice each one, there's a thought, and let it go on without you.
If you find you've boarded one and are a few stops down the line in a story, that's fine. Just step off and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: No-thought. Huineng's teaching that the mind can meet every thought without being carried off by any of them. Not blankness. Today's word.

orig.note: Chinese (wunian): 'no-thought', the first of Huineng's three teachings in the Platform Sutra.

carryVoice: Your line: not stuck. Thoughts can come and go, like trains, without taking you along. Catch you tomorrow.
